system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- For GROUNDED, use "hold" when unreadable PDF symbols prevent verification; explain what is needed. Use fail only when the available evidence is sufficient to determine that the claim is unsupported. This hold rule takes precedence over the strictness rule. Judge other checks independently using their listed values; do not invent missing facts.
- Be strict within each check's allowed values. Do not turn an inability to verify GROUNDED into revise or fail; use hold as defined above.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail / hold]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom, including its specificity, causal force, assumptions, and certainty. pass = fully stated. revise = partly stated (the atom adds, drops, or strengthens something; say what). fail = not stated when the available evidence permits a judgment. hold = unreadable symbols prevent verification. For pass or revise, put the supporting evidence ids in cite.
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately. Evidence spanning more than three sentences is not by itself a reason to split or revise an atom.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge. fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = an isolated study finding, conjecture, or author-specific opinion, classification, or recommendation, even if attribution was removed. Explicitly scoped established facts about a formalism or architecture and conditional theoretical results remain eligible.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a topic whose assessable content is restricted to excluded study-specific findings or author-specific positions. A named formalism, system, or architecture is not disqualified solely for being specific if its scoped conceptual facts are source-independent.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}

CONCEPT: Exploration trap
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: The Ω(log n) memory lower bound for a single deterministic agent in edge-colored graphs. Covers fully regular graphs, the periodic color sequence, and folding to close a loop. Excludes the maze/pebble history.

ATOMS:
- CS-ALG-C02-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: A trap for a deterministic exploration algorithm is an edge-colored graph together with an initial location $v_0$ such that the algorithm, when started at $v_0$, never visits all vertices of the graph.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0168-s08] A trap for an exploration algorithm is given by an edge-colored graph G together with an initial location v0, such that the algorithm never visits all vertices of G when starting at v0.
- CS-ALG-C02-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: An agent with insufficient memory can fail to explore a graph in finite time essentially only by getting trapped in periodic behavior that forces it to move eternally on a closed tour without having visited all vertices.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0164-s01] The Space Complexity of Undirected Graph Exploration
    [CS-ALG-p0168-s05] To approach the question of how much memory is necessary in general to deterministi- cally explore a graph G of size n, we ﬁrst need to realize how insufﬁcient memory can manifest itself in terms of the inability of the agent to explore: Essentially, the only way that the agent may fail to explore G in ﬁnite time is by getting “trapped” in periodic behavior that forces it to move on a closed tour eternally, without having visited all vertices.
- CS-ALG-C02-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: The size of a trap constructed for a deterministic algorithm with a finite number $b$ of memory bits bounds the largest graph size that the algorithm can explore.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0168-s09] We ﬁx a deterministic exploration algorithm A with a ﬁnite number b ∈N of memory bits and construct a trap of some size n for this algorithm.
    [CS-ALG-p0168-s10] The size of our trap then bounds the largest size of graphs that the algorithm can explore.
- CS-ALG-C02-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: Because an algorithm with $b$ memory bits has at most $2^b$ memory states, it must enter some state a second time within its first $2^b$ steps, so its color sequence becomes periodic, $S=(c_1,\dots,c_{i-1})\oplus S_p^\infty$ with $|S_p|=j-i$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0168-s12] To construct a trap G for A , ﬁrst observe that A has at most 2b different memory states at its disposal.
    [CS-ALG-p0168-s15] Since A has at most 2b different states, it must enter at least one state for the second time within the ﬁrst 2b steps.
    [CS-ALG-p0168-s16] Assume the same state is entered in steps 1 ≤i < j ≤2b.
    [CS-ALG-p0168-s17] Then the behavior of A and, consequently, S must become periodic after step i, i.e.,S = (c1,...,ci−1) ⊕S∞p , where ’⊕’ denotes concatenation of sequences, and Sp is a ﬁnite subsequence of S of length j −i.
- CS-ALG-C02-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: For a deterministic algorithm with $b$ memory bits, the trap is built as a fully regular graph of degree 3 with a fixed set of three colors, on which the algorithm produces the same color sequence $S$ irrespective of the initial location.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0168-s13] Our construction ensures that G is a fully regular graph of degree 3, using a ﬁxed set of three colorsC.
    [CS-ALG-p0168-s14] As observed in the previous section, A is sure to yield the same sequence S of colors for all fully regular graphs using colors C and irrespective of the initial location v0.
- CS-ALG-C02-S2-03 | S2
  ATOM: If the walk induced by the color sequence in the infinite 3-regular tree has $v_i=v_j$, the algorithm moves on a closed tour of length $j-i$ after step $i$ having visited at most $j\le 2^b$ vertices, and the subgraph induced by edges incident to the walk's vertices serves as a trap once made fully regular.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0168-s21] Assume that vi = vj.
    [CS-ALG-p0168-s22] Then, the algorithm moves on a closed tour of length j −i after step i while having visited at most i + j −i = j ≤2b differ- ent vertices.
    [CS-ALG-p0168-s23] We can now take the subgraph G of the inﬁnite tree induced by all edges incident to vertices in W as our trap.
- CS-ALG-C02-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: The subgraph induced by the walk's incident edges need not be fully regular, so missing edges are added by mirroring the graph and connecting corresponding vertex pairs of degree smaller than three by an edge of a missing color, which needs to be repeated at most once.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0168-s23] We can now take the subgraph G of the inﬁnite tree induced by all edges incident to vertices in W as our trap.
    [CS-ALG-p0168-s24] Note that this graph need not be fully regular, but we can add missing edges by mirroring G as before (cf.
    [CS-ALG-p0168-s25] Sect. 2) and connecting corre- sponding vertex pairs of degree smaller three by an edge of a color they are missing.
    [CS-ALG-p0168-s26] This decreases the number of missing colors at all vertices of degree smaller three and needs to be repeated at most once to make the graph fully regular.
- CS-ALG-C02-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: The trap construction yields a trap of size $n=O(2^b)$ for any deterministic algorithm with $b$ memory bits, which implies that $\Omega(\log n)$ memory bits are required to explore every graph of size up to $n$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0169-s10] In either case, we have constructed a trap of size n = O (2b).
    [CS-ALG-p0169-s11] Since we can perform this construction for any deterministic algorithm with b memory bits, this implies a lower bound of Ω (logn) on the required number of memory bits to explore every graph of size up to n ∈N.
- CS-ALG-C02-S3-03 | S3
  ATOM: Simply replacing the edge of color $c_{j+1}$ at $v_j$ by the edge $\{v_j,v_{i+1}\}$ cannot close the loop when $v_i\ne v_j$, because the edge $\{v_i,v_{i+1}\}$ of that color must also be kept.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0168-s29] Of course, we cannot simply replace the edge of color cj+1 at vj by the edge {vj,vi+1} of the same color, since we also need to keep the edge {vi,vi+1} of this color.
- CS-ALG-C02-S3-04 | S3
  ATOM: The trap's subgraph need not be fully regular, so missing edges are added by mirroring the graph and connecting corresponding vertex pairs of degree smaller than three by an edge of a missing color, repeated at most once.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0168-s23] We can now take the subgraph G of the inﬁnite tree induced by all edges incident to vertices in W as our trap.
    [CS-ALG-p0168-s24] Note that this graph need not be fully regular, but we can add missing edges by mirroring G as before (cf.
    [CS-ALG-p0168-s25] Sect. 2) and connecting corre- sponding vertex pairs of degree smaller three by an edge of a color they are missing.
    [CS-ALG-p0168-s26] This decreases the number of missing colors at all vertices of degree smaller three and needs to be repeated at most once to make the graph fully regular.
- CS-ALG-C02-S3-05 | S3
  ATOM: The $\Omega(\log n)$ lower bound is tight, since undirected graphs with $n$ vertices can be explored deterministically with $O(\log n)$ memory via Reingold's result that USTCON is in L.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0169-s16] We will see that the lower bound shown in Sect. 3 on the memory needed to explore an undirected graph deterministically is tight, i.e.,undirected graphs with n vertices can be explored deterministically with O (logn) memory.
    [CS-ALG-p0169-s17] This algorithmic result follows from a famous result of Reingold [16] in which he established that USTCON ∈L .
